tasks.title: Reading the Executors Page — One Tab, Five Signals

description.context: A NordGrid mid-level engineer is investigating slow daily-billing pipeline runs. Senior asks them to open the Spark UI's Executors tab and walk through what they see. The cluster has 5 executors running a 12M-row sort-merge aggregation. The Executors page shows per-executor metrics. The engineer needs to interpret five signals at once and identify which executor is in trouble.
description.task: Which executor is in trouble, and what is the dominant signal?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Executor Count: 5

Executor Memory: 8g per executor

Stage: Sort-merge aggregation by region of 12M meter rows

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Spark UI Executors tab snapshot from a 12M-row aggregation pipeline; 5 executors with mixed health signals

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
Spark UI → Executors tab snapshot

Executor   Peak Heap   GC Time    Task Time   Shuffle Read   Container Kills
1          4.2 GB      18 sec     240 sec     580 MB         0
2          4.1 GB      22 sec     250 sec     590 MB         0
3          4.0 GB      19 sec     245 sec     575 MB         0
4          7.8 GB      220 sec    280 sec     6.2 GB         0
5          4.1 GB      20 sec     248 sec     590 MB         0

fields.label: Which executor is in trouble, and what is the dominant signal?
options: All five are healthy. Peak heap below 8 GB on all, no container kills, GC within tolerance. Executor 4's higher numbers reflect a slightly less-balanced shuffle but within Spark's tolerance band.
Executor 4. The 0 container kills is misleading — kills only register after the task finishes. The 7.8 GB peak heap and 220 sec GC are precursor signals to a kill that has not yet happened.
Executors 1, 2, 3, 5. Their ~4 GB peak on 8 GB heap suggests Spark's Tungsten allocator wastes 50% on alignment padding. Fix: enable spark.memory.offHeap.enabled to bypass alignment.
Executor 4. The dominant signal is GC Time at 220 sec — 79% of task time. The shuffle read of 6.2 GB (10× the others) fills the heap to 7.8 GB and forces constant GC. The root cause is data skew.
fields.correctAnswer: Executor 4. The dominant signal is GC Time at 220 sec — 79% of task time. The shuffle read of 6.2 GB (10× the others) fills the heap to 7.8 GB and forces constant GC. The root cause is data skew.
fields.rationale: Reading the Executors tab requires comparing rows. Four executors show consistent metrics; executor 4 is the outlier on every column: 7.8 GB heap (95%), 220 sec GC (79% of task time), 6.2 GB shuffle read (10×). The signals reinforce each other and trace to one cause — a hash partition that is structurally larger than the others. The dominant signal is GC time because that is what shows up in runtime impact.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats a 10× shuffle read imbalance as 'within tolerance'. Spark's tolerance band is roughly 2×; 10× is structural skew.

Option B: Treats 0 container kills as misleading. Kills register correctly; their absence means executor 4 is suffering, not yet dying.

Option C: Invents a Tungsten alignment overhead myth. 50% heap headroom is healthy, not waste.

tasks.pssReference: PSI8 lesson 3 (OOM Diagnosis from Executor Metrics), PSI9 lesson 4 (Reading the Executors Tab).

tasks.title: GC Time of 4 Minutes per Task — What Does It Mean?

description.context: Two NordGrid pipelines have similar runtimes but different GC profiles. Pipeline A's Spark UI shows 4 minutes of GC time on EVERY executor across all tasks. Pipeline B's Spark UI shows 4 minutes of GC time on ONE executor only. The senior engineer asks: same number, different shape — which is which problem?
description.task: Which pipeline has cluster-wide GC pressure and which has per-executor skew?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Task Count: 200

Executor Count: 5

Wall Clock: ~12 min on each pipeline

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Two GC profiles distinguishing cluster-wide pressure from per-executor heap skew

fields.label: Which pipeline has cluster-wide GC pressure and which has per-executor skew?
options: A is cluster-wide pressure (uniform high heap and GC across all workers). B is partition imbalance (only worker 3 elevated). The clue is whether GC is uniform or concentrated on one worker.
Both show cluster-wide GC pressure; the difference is just magnitude. A's 240 sec across 5 executors equals B's 240 sec on one — same total JVM cost. The same fix applies: raise --executor-memory.
B has cluster-wide pressure (the single executor at 240 sec drags the whole stage). A has per-executor skew (each executor has its own load profile, visible in heap and shuffle-read columns).
Neither has either condition; both show normal execution with GC within tolerance. The 240 sec is misleading because the column shows CUMULATIVE GC across the application, not per-task GC.
fields.correctAnswer: A is cluster-wide pressure (uniform high heap and GC across all workers). B is partition imbalance (only worker 3 elevated). The clue is whether GC is uniform or concentrated on one worker.
fields.rationale: The diagnostic question is where GC time is CONCENTRATED. Pipeline A shows uniform high values across all 5 executors — every executor is heap-pressured and constantly garbage-collecting. The 8 GB heap is undersized for the per-executor data volume. Pipeline B concentrates the burden on executor 3 (240 sec GC, 7.9 GB heap, 6.0 GB shuffle read); the others are healthy. Concentration on one executor means data skew. Reading the SHAPE distinguishes the two; the total number alone cannot.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Sums GC time across executors. The shape (concentrated vs spread) carries the diagnostic, not the total.

Option C: Inverts the mapping. Concentrated values mean skew; uniform values mean cluster pressure.

Option D: Misreads the column as cumulative-application. It is cumulative-per-executor, the right unit.

tasks.pssReference: PSI8 lesson 1 (Spark's Memory Architecture), PSI9 lesson 5 (Cluster-Wide vs Per-Executor Pressure).

tasks.title: Skew Shape vs GC Shape vs Spill Shape

description.context: Three NordGrid pipelines have the same wall-clock runtime (~12 min) but three different per-task duration histograms. The senior engineer pastes all three in a Slack thread and asks the team: same runtime, three different shapes, three different fixes. Which is which?
description.task: Which is skew, which is cluster-wide GC, and which is spill?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Task Count Each: 200

Wall Clock Each: ~12 min

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Three per-task duration histograms representing three distinct memory-and-skew failure modes

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
Histogram A — per-task duration
  Min  P25   P50   P75   Max     Tasks
  2s   2.5s  2.6s  3.0s  12min   200
  Tasks 0-196: 2-3 sec
  Tasks 197-199: 12 min each

Histogram B — per-task duration
  Min     P25     P50     P75     Max     Tasks
  3.2min  3.5min  3.6min  3.8min  4.1min  200
  All 200 tasks: 3-4 min, very tight distribution

Histogram C — per-task duration
  Min  P25   P50   P75   Max   Tasks
  55s  62s   75s   3min  4min  200
  ~150 tasks: 1-2 min
  ~50 tasks: 3-4 min (with elevated spill metrics)

fields.label: Which is skew, which is cluster-wide GC, and which is spill?
options: A is GC pressure (3 outliers stuck in long pauses), B is skew (uniform high duration = same large work per task), C is spill (tight P25-P75 with high max). The diagnostic is the absolute max.
A is spill (3 tasks pushed to disk), B is skew (every task hit the same slow path), C is GC (gradual slowdown from accumulating heap pressure). Sudden vs gradual distinguishes spill vs GC.
A is skew (3 tasks far slower; canonical long-tail). B is cluster-wide GC (uniform high duration). C is spill (elevated mean with moderate max plus elevated spill metrics on slow tasks).
All three show the same problem — slow tasks. Same fix applies to all: enable AQE skew handling, which addresses any tail-heavy distribution by splitting slow partitions automatically.
fields.correctAnswer: A is skew (3 tasks far slower; canonical long-tail). B is cluster-wide GC (uniform high duration). C is spill (elevated mean with moderate max plus elevated spill metrics on slow tasks).
fields.rationale: The shape carries the diagnostic. Histogram A's 240× outlier ratio is the canonical SKEW shape — most tasks finish fast, a few dominant key values produce the long tail. Histogram B's uniform-high distribution rules out skew (skew concentrates work) and points to cluster-wide GC pressure where every task pays the same heap overhead. Histogram C's elevated mean with a tail and elevated spill metrics is the SPILL shape — most tasks fit in memory, some exceed and write to disk. Each shape needs a different fix.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Inverts the mapping. Long-tail outliers (A) are skew, not GC; uniform duration (B) is cluster pressure, not skew.

Option B: Swaps spill and GC. Spill produces the elevated-mean-with-tail (C); GC produces the uniform-high (B).

Option D: Collapses three shapes into one fix. AQE skew handling addresses skew shape only.

tasks.pssReference: PSI3 lesson 4 (Data Skew detection), PSI8 lesson 8 (Spill and Disk I/O), PSI9 lesson 4 (Reading Per-Task Distributions).

tasks.title: Per-Task Distribution at 200/200 Tasks Equal — Slow Anyway

description.context: A NordGrid mid-level engineer's pipeline takes 30 minutes when the senior expects 8. The Spark UI Stages page shows 200 tasks all completing in roughly the same time (8.5–9.2 min each, 200/200 evenly distributed). No outliers. No skew. The senior asks: this looks healthy on paper but it is 4× too slow.
description.task: What does the equal-but-slow shape with elevated spill tell you?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Task Count: 200

Executor Count: 4

Executor Memory: 4g each

Expected Runtime: ~8 min

Actual Runtime: 30+ min

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Spark UI per-task distribution showing tight uniform high duration on a 12M-row groupBy with no skew

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
Stage 4 — groupBy('date') over 12M meter rows

Tasks    Min      P25      P50      P75      Max     Skew?
200      8.5min   8.6min   8.8min   9.0min   9.2min  No (tight, 200/200 equal)

Executors: 4
Executor memory: 4g each
Per-task spill bytes: 1.8 GB average
Spill events per task: 4-6 (avg 5)
Shuffle write per task: 60 MB

Expected stage time: ~8 min
Actual stage time: 30+ min

fields.label: What does the equal-but-slow shape with elevated spill tell you?
options: Hidden skew that the histogram is hiding by showing max but not the long tail. Fix: enable spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled to surface the hidden skew via AQE skew handling.
Uniform spill across all tasks — every task's working set exceeds executor memory, every task spills to disk, disk I/O dominates. Fix: raise --executor-memory OR increase shuffle partitions.
Network bottleneck — the 4 executors saturate cluster bandwidth during shuffle read, so each task waits for shuffle blocks. Fix: enable spark.shuffle.compress=true to reduce on-the-wire bytes.
The pipeline is healthy and 30 min is correct for 12M rows on 4 executors; the 8 min expectation is unrealistic. Fix the SLA in team docs, not the code.
fields.correctAnswer: Uniform spill across all tasks — every task's working set exceeds executor memory, every task spills to disk, disk I/O dominates. Fix: raise --executor-memory OR increase shuffle partitions.
fields.rationale: 200 tasks at uniform ~9 min with 1.8 GB average spill and 5 spill events per task — the spill metrics are the smoking gun. Spill happens when a task's working set exceeds memory; Spark serializes to local disk and reads it back. Disk I/O is ~100× slower than memory. The shape is uniform because the spill is uniform — every task has the same working set, every task exceeds memory the same way. Skew would produce a long-tail; cluster-wide GC pressure would lack spill metrics; uniform-high WITH spill is the spill signature.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Invents 'hidden skew' that the data contradicts. 200/200 equal duration rules out skew.

Option C: Misreads spill bytes as network bytes. Spill is local-disk I/O; network has separate metrics.

Option D: Accepts elevated runtime as a fixed cost. The spill metric shows fixable inefficiency.

tasks.pssReference: PSI8 lesson 8 (Spill and Disk I/O), PSI9 lesson 4 (Reading Per-Task Distributions).

tasks.title: Reading an AQE-Engaged Plan

description.context: A NordGrid mid-level engineer's pipeline runs faster than expected. The senior says "AQE engaged at runtime — let me show you what it did." The post-execution explain output shows AQE markers, AQEShuffleRead operators in different modes, and runtime-rewritten partition counts. The engineer must read the plan and identify what AQE did at each marker.
description.task: What three things did AQE do at runtime?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Left Size: 12M rows (meters)

Right Size: 3M rows raw, ~50K after ACTIVE filter (customer_master)

Aqe Settings: enabled with skewJoin and coalescePartitions

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Adaptive plan with three AQE interventions visible in the post-execution explain output

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
result = (meters
    .join(customer_master.filter(col('status') == 'ACTIVE'),
          on='customer_id', how='inner')
    .groupBy('region')
    .agg(sum('daily_kw').alias('total_kw')))
result.explain()

fields.label: What three things did AQE do at runtime?
options: Nothing at runtime; the AdaptiveSparkPlan markers and AQEShuffleRead operators are placeholders that AQE inserts in every adaptive plan whether or not it acts. The plan would look identical without AQE enabled.
(1) Coalesced 200 → 12 partitions because actual partial-aggregate output was smaller than estimated. (2) Split a skewed partition on meters 1 → 8. (3) Converted sort-merge to broadcast at runtime.
Skipped the join entirely because runtime statistics showed the result would be empty; the BroadcastExchange is a stub that emits zero rows. The 200 → 12 coalesce reflects the empty result.
Only coalesced shuffle partitions; the BroadcastHashJoin and skew split are NOT AQE — they are Catalyst-time decisions that look like AQE because of overlapping operator names in the plan output.
fields.correctAnswer: (1) Coalesced 200 → 12 partitions because actual partial-aggregate output was smaller than estimated. (2) Split a skewed partition on meters 1 → 8. (3) Converted sort-merge to broadcast at runtime.
fields.rationale: Reading top-down identifies three interventions. AQEShuffleRead coalesced (200 → 12) merged adjacent small partitions because regions are low-cardinality after partial aggregation. AQEShuffleRead local (skew partition split: 1 → 8) split a skewed customer_id bucket for parallel processing. BroadcastExchange built from runtime-collected 50K rows shows AQE rewrote the planned sort-merge to broadcast because the post-filter size was below threshold. isFinalPlan=true confirms AQE completed.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats AQE markers as inert. The numeric labels (200 → 12, 1 → 8) record actual rewrites.

Option C: Invents a 'skip the join' optimization. AQE does not skip joins; the plan shows the join executed.

Option D: Misattributes skew split and BHJ to Catalyst-time. Both depend on runtime data Catalyst cannot observe.

tasks.pssReference: PSI1 lesson 8 (Adaptive Query Execution Overview), PSI3 lesson 6 (Resolving Skew with AQE).

tasks.title: AQE Skew Handling Did Not Engage — Why?

description.context: A NordGrid mid-level engineer is investigating a slow pipeline. The Spark UI shows obvious skew: 197 tasks finish in 2 min, 3 tasks take 90+ min. The cluster has spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=true and spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled=true. AQE skew handling SHOULD have engaged but did not.
description.task: Why did AQE skew handling fail to engage?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Observed Skew Factor: 60× (well above the 5× default)

Per Skewed Partition Size: 12 GB (well above 256MB default)

Join Type: LEFT OUTER JOIN

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Pipeline with obvious skew where AQE skew handling failed to engage despite being enabled

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
# Pipeline:
result = (meters
    .join(events_log, on='meter_id', how='left')
    .groupBy('region')
    .agg(sum('event_count').alias('total_events')))

# Observed:
#   Spark UI: 197 tasks at 2 min, 3 tasks at 90+ min
#   skew factor: 60× (well above 5× default)
#   per-skewed-partition size: 12 GB (well above 256MB default)
#
# Cluster config:
#   spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=true
#   spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled=true
#   spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionFactor=5
#
# Plan post-execution:
#   AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=true
#   SortMergeJoin [meter_id], [meter_id], LeftOuter
#   No AQEShuffleRead local (skew partition split) anywhere

fields.label: Why did AQE skew handling fail to engage?
options: Skewed partitions over 8GB are 'too large to safely split'; the 12GB partitions trigger an internal AQE bailout. Fix: manually salt the join key before the shuffle.
AQE skew handling does NOT support LEFT OUTER (or RIGHT/FULL OUTER) — only INNER and one direction. The 'how=left' falls outside the supported set, so AQE silently skips. Fix: salt manually.
AQE measures compressed shuffle sizes; the 12GB is post-decompression, so AQE thinks the partitions are below threshold. Fix: disable spark.sql.shuffle.compress so AQE sees true sizes.

AQE skew handling only runs on the FIRST shuffle stage of an application; the join's shuffle is the second stage (after the .filter() shuffle). Fix: remove the upstream filter or move it after the join.
fields.correctAnswer: AQE skew handling does NOT support LEFT OUTER (or RIGHT/FULL OUTER) — only INNER and one direction. The 'how=left' falls outside the supported set, so AQE silently skips. Fix: salt manually.
fields.rationale: AQE skew handling has a join-type support matrix. INNER joins are fully supported. LEFT OUTER is supported only when the LEFT side has the skew AND the RIGHT side is being scanned. FULL OUTER is not supported. When the join type is incompatible, AQE silently skips — no warning, no log, just absent operators. This is the most common reason AQE skew handling fails in practice. Fix: manually salt (engineer takes over the split) or restructure to INNER + null-handling.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Invents an 8GB upper bailout. AQE has size thresholds for triggering, not for skipping at the high end.

Option C: Invents a compression-heuristic interaction. AQE measures bytes-on-disk after compression, the right unit.

Option D: Invents a 'first shuffle only' rule. AQE acts on every shuffle stage.

tasks.pssReference: PSI3 lesson 6 (Resolving Skew with AQE — limitations), PSI3 lesson 5 (Salting as fallback).

tasks.title: Salting Factor Calculation — Two Approaches Compared

description.context: Two NordGrid mid-level engineers solve the same skew problem differently. The pipeline aggregates 12M meter rows by customer_type, where customer_type follows the 60/25/12/3 NordGrid distribution. Both engineers add salting to spread the skewed RESIDENTIAL key. Engineer A picks salt factor 10. Engineer B computes the salt factor based on the data distribution.
description.task: Which salt factor is correct, and what is the cost trade-off?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Key Distribution: RESIDENTIAL 60%, COMMERCIAL 25%, INDUSTRIAL 12%, PROSUMER 3%

Shuffle Partitions: 200

Rows Per Task Target: ~60K rows (12M / 200)

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Two salting implementations with different salt factors against NordGrid customer_type distribution

fields.label: Which salt factor is correct, and what is the cost trade-off?
options: A (factor 10) is correct — 10 is the canonical default. Salt factor 120 over-engineers and produces 12× more output rows in partial aggregation, slowing post-aggregation by 12×.
Both equivalent in correctness; salt factor only affects parallelism. A produces 4×10=40 partial buckets, B produces 4×120=480; pick A as cheaper at this scale and same final result.
B (factor 120) is correct. RESIDENTIAL = 60% × 12M = 7.2M rows in ONE bucket. Factor 10 → 720K per bucket, still 12× target. Factor 120 → 60K per bucket, matching target.

Neither — salt factor must be a power of 2 (8, 16, 32, 64, 128) for Spark's hash to distribute evenly. Both 10 and 120 produce hash collisions. Correct factor: 128 (closest power of 2 to B's calculation).
fields.correctAnswer: B (factor 120) is correct. RESIDENTIAL = 60% × 12M = 7.2M rows in ONE bucket. Factor 10 → 720K per bucket, still 12× target. Factor 120 → 60K per bucket, matching target.
fields.rationale: Salting works by splitting one skewed key into N synthetic keys. The right N depends on the data. RESIDENTIAL = 60% × 12M = 7.2M rows; target per task = 60K. Factor 10 leaves 720K per bucket — still 12× target, still skew. Factor 120 splits to 60K per bucket — equal to target. Formula: salt_factor = dominant_share / minor_share. The over-salting cost (480 vs 40 partial buckets) is logarithmic; the savings from eliminating skew are linear. B wins by a large margin.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Reverses cost-benefit. Over-salting cost is logarithmic; under-salting leaves linear skew cost.

Option B: Treats salt as parallelism only. Salt factor is the structural lever for whether skew is eliminated.

Option D: Invents power-of-2 requirement. Spark's hash distributes uniformly modulo any positive integer.

tasks.pssReference: PSI3 lesson 5 (Resolving Skew with Salting), PSI3 lesson 5b (Salt Factor Calculation).

tasks.title: The Salt That Disappeared After AQE

description.context: A NordGrid mid-level engineer added hand-rolled salting to their join eight months ago to handle customer_type skew. The pipeline worked correctly when AQE was disabled. After Platform enabled AQE by default last month, the same pipeline started producing rows with NULL on the salted_dim columns — not consistently, but enough to fail downstream validation. The cascade of failed retries triggers executor OOMs that the engineer initially misdiagnoses as memory pressure. Cross-references PJSI4.2 (joins angle).
description.task: What is the bug, why do executor OOMs appear, and why does raising --executor-memory not fix them?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Salt Factor: 10

Aqe State: enabled cluster-default since last month

Primary Failure: intermittent NULLs in salted_dim columns post-join

Secondary Failure: executor OOMs on stage retries; raising --executor-memory does not help

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Hand-rolled salting code interacting with AQE-enabled cluster; cross-track reprise of the join symptom as a memory cascade

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, expr, lit, concat

# Salt the meters side: append random 0-9 suffix
salted_meters = meters.withColumn(
    'customer_type_salted',
    concat(col('customer_type'), lit('_'),
           (expr('rand() * 10').cast('int'))))

# Replicate the dim side: 10 rows per customer_type
salted_dim = (customer_type_dim
    .crossJoin(spark.range(10).withColumnRenamed('id', 'salt'))
    .withColumn('customer_type_salted',
        concat(col('customer_type'), lit('_'), col('salt').cast('int'))))

# Join on the salted key
result = salted_meters.join(salted_dim, on='customer_type_salted', how='left')

fields.label: What is the bug, why do executor OOMs appear, and why does raising --executor-memory not fix them?
options: Shuffle buffer running out during the salt-driven repartition; --executor-memory should help but spark.shuffle.memoryFraction is set too low to actually use the additional heap. Fix: raise spark.shuffle.memoryFraction.

rand() is non-deterministic. AQE re-evaluation may run salting with new values. salted_meters and salted_dim then mismatch. Joins miss → retries → tasks pile on survivors → OOMs. Fix: pmod(crc32(meter_id), 10).

The crossJoin produces 10× rows on the dim side; inflation forces sort-merge instead of broadcast, sort-merge spills, spill triggers OOMs. Fix: broadcast the dim side explicitly with broadcast() hint.

AQE's coalesce-shuffle-partitions reduced the partition count below 10, mapping multiple salt values to the same partition; the salt's pre-condition is invalidated. Fix: disable AQE for this stage with /*+ NO_AQE */.
fields.correctAnswer: rand() is non-deterministic. AQE re-evaluation may run salting with new values. salted_meters and salted_dim then mismatch. Joins miss → retries → tasks pile on survivors → OOMs. Fix: pmod(crc32(meter_id), 10).
fields.rationale: rand() is non-deterministic. AQE's plan re-evaluation may execute the salting expression with new random values; salted_meters and salted_dim then hold mismatched salts. Joins on mismatched-salt rows produce NULLs. Validation failures trigger retries; retries re-run salting with new rand() values, creating new mismatches. Tasks accumulate on surviving executors and eventually OOM. Raising --executor-memory delays the OOM but does not stop the cascade. Fix: use pmod(crc32(meter_id), 10) — deterministic across re-evaluations.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Cites spark.shuffle.memoryFraction, which was deprecated in Spark 1.6+.

Option C: Confuses crossJoin row inflation (real concern) with the cause of NULLs (rand() non-determinism).

Option D: Treats partition coalescing as invalidating the salt. Coalesce is partition-level; salt is data-level.

tasks.pssReference: PSI3 lesson 5 (Salting), PSI3 lesson 6 (AQE limitations), PSI8 lesson 3 (OOM Diagnosis — root cause vs cascade). Cross-reference: PJSI4.2 covers the same root cause from the join-correctness angle.

tasks.title: Aggregation Pipeline With Memory Footprint Audit

description.context: A NordGrid mid-level engineer's daily-aggregation pipeline runs at production scale (12M meters). The senior engineer schedules a memory audit and walks through five targeted questions about the pipeline's memory footprint at each step.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: 50-line aggregation pipeline at 12M-row scale; 5 targeted memory questions across the 5 modules' material

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import (col, sum, broadcast, hash, concat,
                                     lit, abs as f_abs, split)

spark = (SparkSession.builder
    .appName('billing_aggregation')
    .config('spark.executor.memory', '8g')
    .config('spark.executor.memoryOverhead', '1500m')
    .config('spark.sql.adaptive.enabled', 'true')
    .config('spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled', 'true')
    .config('spark.sql.shuffle.partitions', '200')
    .getOrCreate())

# Step 1: load and filter
meters = spark.read.parquet('silver/meters/2026-04-30/')   # 12M rows
active = meters.filter(col('status') == 'ACTIVE')

# Step 2: salt customer_type to handle the 60/25/12/3 skew
#   (engineer chose salt factor 120 based on the 60% dominant share)
salted = active.withColumn('customer_type_salted',
    concat(col('customer_type'), lit('_'),
           (f_abs(hash(col('meter_id'))) % 120).cast('int')))

# Step 3: aggregate at salted level (partial)
partial = salted.groupBy('customer_type_salted', 'region').agg(
    sum('daily_kw').alias('partial_kw'))
partial.cache()

# Step 4: enrich with substations (broadcast eligible)
subs = spark.read.parquet('reference/substations/')   # 200 rows
enriched = partial.join(broadcast(subs), on='region', how='left')

# Step 5: re-aggregate at customer_type level (final)
final = (enriched
    .withColumn('customer_type', split('customer_type_salted', '_')[0])
    .groupBy('customer_type', 'region', 'capacity_mw')
    .agg(sum('partial_kw').alias('total_kw')))

# Step 6: write
final.write.mode('overwrite').partitionBy('region').parquet('gold/billing/')

# Step 7: cleanup
print(f'Pipeline complete; {final.count()} aggregated rows')

tasks.pssReference: PSI3 lessons 4-6 (skew detection and salting), PSI8 lessons 1-6 (memory architecture and cache lifecycle), PSI9 (Performance Monitoring).

tasks.title: The Pipeline With Five Mid-Level Memory-and-Skew Bugs

description.context: Final exercise of the Mid track. A NordGrid pipeline runs without errors but Finance reports billing arrives 4 hours late and Operations reports 'task failed 4 times' alerts. Investigation traces the symptoms to five distinct Mid-level memory-and-skew mistakes in the same 55-line pipeline.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: 55-line daily-billing pipeline at NordGrid Mid scale with five embedded Mid-level memory-and-skew bugs

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import (col, sum, broadcast, expr, lit,
                                     concat, split)

spark = (SparkSession.builder
    .appName('billing')
    .config('spark.executor.memory', '8g')
    .config('spark.executor.memoryOverhead', '400m')
    .config('spark.sql.adaptive.enabled', 'true')
    .config('spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled', 'true')
    .config('spark.sql.shuffle.partitions', '200')
    .config('spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold', '500m')
    .getOrCreate())

# Step 1: load
meters = spark.read.parquet('silver/meters/2026-04-30/')      # 12M rows
customers = spark.read.parquet('reference/customer_master/')  # 3M rows, 280MB

# Step 2: salt for skew (rand-based; salt factor 10)
salted_meters = meters.withColumn('customer_type_salted',
    concat(col('customer_type'), lit('_'),
           (expr('rand() * 10').cast('int'))))

# Step 3: enrich with customer_master
enriched = salted_meters.join(broadcast(customers), on='customer_id', how='left')
enriched.cache()

# Step 4: outer-join to events for fraud detection
events = spark.read.parquet('silver/events/last_30_days/')   # 8M rows
flagged = enriched.join(events, on='meter_id', how='full_outer')

# Step 5: compute revenue (UDF over 12M rows)
from pyspark.sql.functions import udf
from pyspark.sql.types import DoubleType

@udf(returnType=DoubleType())
def compute_revenue(daily_kw, customer_type, region):
    base = daily_kw * 0.18
    multiplier = {'RESIDENTIAL': 1.0, 'COMMERCIAL': 1.3,
                  'INDUSTRIAL': 1.5, 'PROSUMER': 0.85}.get(customer_type, 1.0)
    return base * multiplier

revenue = flagged.withColumn('revenue', compute_revenue(
    col('daily_kw'), col('customer_type_salted'), col('region')))

# Step 6: aggregate to per-region totals
summary = revenue.groupBy('region').agg(
    sum('revenue').alias('total_revenue_eur'))

summary.write.mode('overwrite').partitionBy('region').parquet('gold/billing/')
